value: Compared to the healthy controls, heroin-dependent individuals showed significantly decreased cortical thickness in the bilateral superior frontal, left caudal middle frontal, right insular, and right superior temporal regions, and significantly increased cortical thickness in the bilateral lingual, left superior parietal, left temporal pole, right lateral occipital, right inferior parietal, and right cuneus regions.

The findings indicate that the frontal cortex is vulnerable to heroin addiction, and abnormal cortical thickness in the prefrontal and insular regions may be related to impaired self-control and compulsive drug-taking behavior.

value: The ROI-wise analysis found significantly decreased cortical thickness in nine regions in heroin-dependent individuals compared with healthy controls, including the left precuneus gyrus, left calcarine sulcus, left inferior circular insular sulcus, left superior frontal sulcus, left inferior temporal sulcus, bilateral anterior transverse collateral sulcus, right medial occipital-temporal and lingual sulcus, and right orbital sulci.

The ROI-wise analysis provided a complementary perspective to the vertex-wise findings; both analyses identified abnormalities in the left superior frontal sulcus, left precuneus gyrus, left calcarine sulcus, left anterior transverse collateral sulcus, and right medial occipital-temporal and lingual sulcus.

The longer the duration of heroin use, the thinner the cortical thickness in the right superior frontal and right insular regions, suggesting that duration of heroin use may be a critical factor associated with abnormalities in these regions.
